title: Growing sea kale
subtitle: A hardy UK coastal perennial with forced winter shoots and a long garden life.
excerpt: Sea kale is a native UK perennial grown for its forced shoots in late winter and spring. An established crown produces blanched stems each year for ten years or more. The plant is easy to grow in well-drained soil in full sun.
sourceNotes: Growing method from Gertrude Jekyll's kitchen-garden writing and Mrs Beeton's Book of Household Management (1861). Forcing technique widely documented in Victorian kitchen-garden literature. RHS plant data used for hardiness and spacing.

glossaryTerms.definition: Excluding light from a plant to encourage pale, tender, mild-flavoured growth. Sea kale and rhubarb are forced by covering the crown with a pot or box in late winter; the plant pushes up etiolated shoots that are sweeter and more tender than those grown in full light.
A root cutting from a sea kale or horseradish plant. A section of root 5 to 10 cm long with a dormant bud, used for propagation. More reliable and faster than growing from seed.

content.text: Sea kale is a native UK coastal plant grown for its pale, tender shoots produced in late winter under

Sea kale is native to shingle beaches and sea cliffs. It needs full sun, excellent drainage, and a lean soil. It performs poorly in heavy clay, waterlogged ground, or shade. A raised bed, a slope, or a sandy soil all suit it. Hardy to H7 and very long-lived once established.

Plant thong cuttings in March or April, bud-end up, at 5 cm depth. Space plants 45 to 60 cm apart. Firm in well. Water if dry. Keep weed-free for the first season; the young plants are slow to get going and can be smothered by faster weeds.

In late January or early February, cover each crown with an upturned bucket, terracotta forcing pot, or large plastic pot with the drainage holes blocked. The aim is total light exclusion. The crown warms under the pot and pushes pale, tender shoots upward. Remove the covering after six to eight weeks and harvest the shoots when they are 15 to 20 cm tall.

Do not force every crown every year. Force one or two crowns and leave the others uncovered to build up root reserves. Forced plants produce smaller shoots the following year and need a full season to recover before forcing again.

Cut forced shoots when they reach 15 to 20 cm. They have a mild cabbage-like flavour and a slightly crunchy texture. Eat steamed, boiled, or roasted. The unforced plant produces open-grown shoots in spring and white flowers in May and June; both the shoots and flowers are edible.

Remove the forcing pot once the shoots have been harvested. Allow the crown to produce leaves and build up root reserves through spring and summer. In October, take root cuttings (thongs) from the outer roots to propagate new plants. Store the thongs in just-moist compost over winter and plant them out in March.
